name: Saladin
role: First sultan of Egypt and Syria, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty (r. 1174–1193)
summary: Saladin was a Sunni Kurdish commander who rose as vizier in Fatimid Egypt, ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and united Egypt, Syria and much of Mesopotamia under his rule. His contemporaries record a ruler devoted to the Holy War against the Crusaders, to orthodox Sunni religion and to personal generosity, who sat regularly to hear petitions and who took Jerusalem in 1187. He left no writings on government in general, so his recorded positions mostly concern religion, war and rule.

sources.title: The Life of Saladin (What Befell Sultan Yusuf), PEF/PPTS translation, 1897
sources.author: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad (Saladin's qadi and companion)
sources.usedFor: Eyewitness account of his character, justice sittings, religious views, Suhrawardi execution, Hattin, Jerusalem terms, letters to Richard, peace of 1192 and dying advice to ez-Zaher

sources.title: Saladin and the Fall of the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1898)
sources.author: Stanley Lane-Poole
sources.usedFor: End of the Fatimid caliphate, Sunni colleges, pilgrim tolls, his zeal for jihad and the message to ez-Zaher

sources.title: Saladin
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Identity and dates; abolition of the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and restoration of Abbasid allegiance

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Baha ad-Din, who wrote a treatise on the rules of the Holy War at Saladin's request, reports that Saladin treated jihad against the Franks as his overriding duty, spent his treasury only on it, and reproached Muslim princes for lukewarm support (Lane-Poole). He framed Frankish rule as seizure of Muslim land ('it belonged originally to us'). The exact wording that resistance binds every Muslim is not quoted from him.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Baha ad-Din reports he 'believed steadfastly in all the teaching of the Divine Law', sat twice weekly with judges and jurists to hear petitions, read treatises on jurisprudence, and had a man executed for not recognising the ordinances of the law. He ruled under religious law as a matter of course, though no abstract statement is quoted.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: In his dying advice to his son ez-Zaher, quoted by Baha ad-Din, he said 'thou art only appointed by God and by me' to look after the subjects' good, and he credited God for giving him Egypt and the conquest of the coast. He presented rule as entrusted by God.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Baha ad-Din says he 'detested philosophers, heretics, materialists, and all adversaries of orthodox religion', believed in bodily resurrection, wept when the Qur'an was recited and trusted in God above counsel. He rejected reason as the sole guide.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Baha ad-Din reports that he accepted all the teaching of the Divine Law 'with an open heart' and openly maintained literal doctrines such as bodily resurrection, Paradise and Hell, and opposed rationalist schools. No explicit doctrine of inerrancy is quoted, so medium and +1.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Baha ad-Din describes him ordering his own nephew Taqi ad-Din to appear before the tribunal on a petitioner's complaint, and himself appearing in court as defendant against the merchant 'Omar el-Kheldti, saying he would 'conform to all the regulations prescribed by law'. The law in question was the religious law rather than his own decrees, hence -1.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He installed his sons as rulers in his lifetime (el-Afdal, ez-Zaher at Aleppo) and told Baha ad-Din he meant to 'divide my territories, and charge (my successors) with my last commands'; his parting advice to ez-Zaher is addressed to a son ruling under him. Succession of children was his practice.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Inferred: from his stated plan to divide his dominions among his successors and his appointing his sons as rulers, which presupposes that hereditary rulers can be legitimate. He also served the Abbasid caliph as overlord. He did not discuss monarchy as a principle.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: No recorded position found. (Reviewer: an inference from his family rule and orphan stipends is nearby evidence, not a view on hereditary titles.)

historical-land-claim.rationale: His reply to Richard, quoted by Baha ad-Din: 'Jerusalem belongs to us just as much as to you, and is more precious in our eyes than in yours, for it was the place of our Prophet's journey' and the land 'belonged originally to us'. The claim rests on religious tie and earlier possession over the Franks now holding it, though he says 'as much as' for Jerusalem.

return-lost-territory.rationale: His letter to Richard (Baha ad-Din) insisted that land the Franks took in earlier wars was originally Muslim and that God would not let them raise a stone there while war lasted; his campaigns of 1187 onward aimed to recover Jerusalem and the coast. Treaty of 1192 left most coast to the Franks, hence only +1.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Mixed record. He refused to give up Jerusalem ('we are fully resolved never to give it up'), yet in the 1192 peace he left Jaffa, Caesarea, Acre and the coast to the Franks, which he had claimed as originally Muslim land, because his troops were exhausted.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He conquered Egypt, Syria, much of Upper Mesopotamia and Palestine and told Baha ad-Din that after expelling the Franks he would cross the sea and pursue them until no unbeliever remained. His aim was framed as holy war, not national aggrandisement, hence +1.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He opened the 1187 campaign that led to Hattin and Jerusalem, besieged Zengid and Frankish cities, and said he would pursue unbelievers across the sea (Baha ad-Din). He did not confine force to defence.

political-violence-never.rationale: He waged holy war and civil wars, personally killed Reynald of Chatillon after Hattin, had all captured Templars and Hospitallers executed, and had the Egyptian vizier Shawar beheaded after arrest (Baha ad-Din). He plainly held that political violence can be justified, though he told his son to be wary of shedding blood.

death-penalty.rationale: No recorded position found. (Reviewer: summary killings of captives are nearby evidence, not a view on executing the convicted.)

apostasy-punishable.rationale: No recorded position found. (Reviewer: the Suhrawardi execution was for heresy, which is nearby evidence, not a view on leaving one's religion.)

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Same Suhrawardi case (he 'detested ... heretics'): the execution for alleged unbelief shows he allowed state punishment of heterodox speech. Against that, he allowed Christians to keep the Church of the Resurrection and pilgrimage under the 1192 treaty, so contested and low.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Baha ad-Din reports he cared for orphans (continuing their father's pay and arranging upbringing), gave away provinces and nearly all his wealth, and left 47 dirhems. His own advice to his son: watch over the subjects' interests because 'thou art only appointed ... to look after their good'.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: He described his wars as fighting for God against unbelief ('I strive for the door of the most glorious of deaths') and wished to purge the earth of unbelievers (Baha ad-Din). He did not use the wording 'good and evil' for politics generally, hence low.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Mixed. He held even his nephew and himself answerable in court and heard petitions from 'great and small', but Baha ad-Din also records that he saw a difference between Muslim and infidel, and ransom terms and treatment varied by faith.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: He ended the Ismaili Fatimid caliphate in 1171, had the Friday prayer said for the Abbasid caliph, and founded Sunni colleges and teachers in Cairo and provincial towns to restore Sunni teaching (Lane-Poole; Baha ad-Din: he 'took great pains to establish the true faith (sunna) more firmly').

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: No recorded position found. (Reviewer: founding Sunni religious colleges is nearby evidence, not a view on state schools.)

notes: Wikipedia gives his birth as c. 1137 (the catalogue says 1138); he died 4 March 1193. Almost every answer rests on Baha ad-Din's near-contemporary account, so confidence is medium at most; no WebSearch used. Executions at Hattin and of Suhrawardi are recorded but the motives are partly political.
